title: Arrays & Hashing
tagline: The O(1) lookup lever that unlocks ~40% of interview questions.
intro:
Arrays and hash maps together account for roughly 40% of easy and medium coding-interview problems, and they are the foundation almost every other pattern builds on. An **array** gives you O(1) access *by position*; a **hash map** gives you O(1) access *by value*. Master the move from one to the other and a huge slice of the interview pool collapses into a single mental model.

The core insight is this: a hash map turns the question "have I seen the value x before?" from an O(n) scan into an O(1) lookup. So a nested-loop O(n²) brute force becomes a single linear O(n) pass. You are trading O(n) extra space for an order-of-magnitude time saving — almost always the right trade in an interview unless you are explicitly told space is constrained.

This module teaches the four levers you will reach for again and again: the **one-pass hash map** (Two Sum and its cousins), **frequency counting** (anagrams, top-K, majority), **prefix sums** (subarray-sum range queries), and **set membership** (duplicates, uniqueness). Each section gives you the definition, a diagram of how it works, the dual-language template, and the interview talking points.
objectives: Choose correctly between array, hash set, and hash map for any given problem
Explain how a hash table achieves O(1) average lookup — and when it degrades to O(n)
Write one-pass O(n) traversals that use a hash map as the "memory"
Apply the two-sum template to any "find two elements that satisfy X" problem
Use frequency counting for anagrams, duplicates, top-K, and majority problems
Apply prefix sums to convert range-sum queries from O(n) to O(1)
Recognise when sorting or two pointers beats hashing (sorted input, or O(1) space required)

signals: "Find two elements that sum to ..." / "Find a pair that ..."
"Count subarrays with sum equal to k" → prefix sum + hash map
antiSignals: Input is already sorted → two pointers is usually cheaper in space
"No extra space" / "in-place" constraint → hashing is disqualified, sort or two-pointer instead
"Contiguous subarray with a window condition" → probably sliding window
Constraints are tiny (n ≤ 20) → brute force is fine, don't over-engineer

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Imagine a coat-check counter. You hand over your coat (a value) and get a numbered ticket (a key); later you show the ticket and instantly get your coat back without searching the whole rack. A hash map works the same way - it jumps straight to what you stored instead of scanning everything.

That one trick is why so many array problems get fast. Example: to find two numbers in `[2, 7, 11, 15]` that add up to 9, walk through once and remember each number you have already seen. At 2 you think 'I still need a 7'. When you reach 7 you ask 'have I seen a 7 before?' - yes - so the pair is found in a single walk instead of comparing every possible pair.

sections.heading: Core definitions — the vocabulary
sections.body:
Before the patterns, lock in the vocabulary. Interviewers listen for whether you use these terms precisely.

| Term | What it means | Typical cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Array** | Contiguous block of memory indexed by position `0..n-1`. | Access by index O(1); search O(n) |
| **Dynamic array** | Auto-resizing array (Java `ArrayList`, Python `list`). Doubles capacity when full. | Append *amortised* O(1) |
| **Hash set** | Unordered collection of unique keys. Answers "is x present?". | Add / contains O(1) average |
| **Hash map** | Key → value store. Answers "what is associated with x?". | Put / get O(1) average |
| **Hash function** | Maps a key to a bucket index. | O(1) per key |
| **Collision** | Two keys hash to the same bucket; resolved by chaining or probing. | Degrades lookup toward O(n) |
| **Load factor** | `size / buckets`. When it crosses a threshold the table resizes. | Triggers O(n) rehash |

The single most important idea: **a hash set tells you *whether* something exists; a hash map tells you *what* is attached to it** (an index, a count, a list). Pick the set when existence is all you need — it is lighter and signals intent.

callouts.text: Java: `HashSet<Integer>` / `HashMap<Integer,Integer>`. Python: `set()` / `dict()` — plus `collections.Counter` for frequencies and `collections.defaultdict(int)` for "initialise to zero" semantics.

sections.heading: How hashing achieves O(1) — and when it doesn't
sections.body:
A hash table stores keys in an array of *buckets*. To find a key it runs the key through a **hash function** to get a bucket index, then looks only inside that bucket — not the whole table. With a good hash function and a low load factor, each bucket holds ~1 item, so lookup is O(1) on average.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  K["key (e.g. 42)"] --> H["hash(key)"]
  H --> M["index = hash % numBuckets"]
  M --> B[("bucket array")]
  B --> V["value / present?"]
```

The catch: if many keys **collide** into one bucket, that bucket becomes a linear list and lookups drift toward O(n). This is why interviewers say hashing is O(1) *average* but O(n) *worst case*. In practice, for interview inputs you treat it as O(1) — but you should be able to state the worst case if asked.

callouts.text: Hash maps have no inherent order. If a problem needs sorted output or order-by-insertion, you'll sort at the end (O(n log n)) or use a `LinkedHashMap` / Python `dict` insertion order.

sections.heading: Choosing the right structure (decision flow)
sections.body:
Most array problems reduce to one decision: *what do I need to remember as I scan, and how do I look it up?* Walk this flow at the start of any array problem.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Relate elements of an array"] --> B{"Input already sorted?"}
  B -- Yes --> C["Two pointers — O(1) space"]
  B -- No --> D{"What must you recall?"}
  D -- "Just existence" --> E["Hash set"]
  D -- "Value → index" --> F["Hash map: value to index"]
  D -- "Counts / frequency" --> G["Hash map / Counter"]
  D -- "Running totals" --> H["Prefix sum + hash map"]
```

This is the question interviewers want to hear you reason through out loud before you write a line of code.

callouts.text: If the prompt says "sorted array" or "O(1) extra space", do **not** default to a hash map — that throws away the property they handed you. Reach for two pointers or binary search instead.

sections.heading: Lever 1 — the one-pass two-sum template
sections.body:
Given an array and a target, find two elements that sum to the target. Brute force is O(n²) nested loops. The one-pass hash map is O(n).

The key reframing: as you iterate, don't ask "does x exist in what I've seen?" — ask "does `target - x` (the **complement**) exist in what I've seen?" Store each value's index as you go, and the first time a complement is already present, you've found the pair. This generalises to any "find a pair that together satisfies a property" problem.

callouts.text: Storing the index *after* checking the complement is what prevents using the same element twice — you only ever match against elements strictly to the left of `i`.

sections.heading: Lever 2 — frequency counting
sections.body:
When the problem asks "how many of each" or "most/least common", build a frequency map: key → count. In Java that's a `HashMap<T,Integer>` with `merge`; in Python it's `collections.Counter`.

Applications: Valid Anagram (two strings share the same frequency map), Top K Frequent, Majority Element, First Unique Character.

sections.heading: Lever 3 — prefix sums for range queries
sections.body:
When the problem involves "sum of a subarray" or "count subarrays with sum = k", prefix sums plus a hash map are almost always the play.

Define `prefix[i]` = sum of `nums[0..i]`. Then the sum of range `(i, j]` = `prefix[j] - prefix[i]`. To count subarrays summing to `k`, ask at each step "how many earlier prefixes equal `currentPrefix - k`?" and keep those counts in a hash map for O(1) lookup. Seed it with `{0: 1}` to represent the empty prefix — forgetting this is the classic off-by-one bug.

codeExamples.label: Subarray sum equals k
codeExamples.code:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count, prefix = 0, 0
    seen = {0: 1}                 # empty prefix has sum 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return count

sections.heading: Variants you'll meet (and the right tool)
sections.body:
Almost every arrays-and-hashing interview question is one of these shapes. Match the prompt to the row and the technique falls out.

| Problem shape | Tool | Canonical example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Find a pair summing to a target | Hash map (value → index) | Two Sum |
| Detect any duplicate | Hash set | Contains Duplicate |
| Same characters, any order | Frequency map compare | Valid Anagram |
| Bucket items by a signature | Map (key → list) | Group Anagrams |
| k most frequent | Counter + heap / bucket sort | Top K Frequent |
| Count / find subarray by sum | Prefix sum + hash map | Subarray Sum Equals K |
| Longest run of consecutive ints | Hash set + boundary check | Longest Consecutive Sequence |

For **Group Anagrams** the grouping key is `tuple(sorted(s))` in Python (or a 26-length frequency tuple); in Java it's a sorted `char[]` rebuilt into a `String`, or an `int[26]` serialised to a key.

sections.heading: Complexity at a glance
sections.body:
Know these cold — you should be able to state them without thinking.

| Operation | Average | Worst case |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hash set / map insert | O(1) | O(n) (all collisions) |
| Hash set / map lookup | O(1) | O(n) |
| One-pass scan with hash map | O(n) time, O(n) space | — |
| Frequency count (fixed alphabet) | O(n) time, **O(1)** space | — |
| Group anagrams | O(n·k log k) | — (k = word length) |
| Sorting fallback | O(n log n) time, O(1)–O(n) space | — |

Frequency counting over a fixed alphabet (e.g. lowercase a–z) is **O(1) space**: the map holds at most 26 entries regardless of input size.

interviewTalking: When you open an array problem that needs a relationship between elements, narrate the trade-off before coding: "Brute force is the nested loop at O(n²). I can trade O(n) space for O(n) time by remembering what I've seen in a hash map — specifically, I'll look up the complement rather than rescan. Unless you want constant extra space, I'll go with the hash map." That one sentence earns the algorithm-choice signal interviewers are grading. Then code the one-pass template and close with the explicit complexity statement: O(n) time, O(n) space.
commonMistakes: Using a hash set when you need the *index* — use a hash map if the problem returns positions
Storing the current element before checking its complement, which lets an element pair with itself
Using `containsKey` + `get` instead of a single `getOrDefault` / `merge` — correct but wordier and slower
Reaching for hashing when the input is already sorted — two pointers is simpler and O(1) space
Forgetting to seed the prefix-sum map with `{0: 1}`, which under-counts subarrays starting at index 0
Claiming hashing is "always O(1)" — say *average* O(1), worst case O(n) under heavy collisions
complexityNotes: One-pass hash-map solutions in this module are O(n) time and O(n) space, where n is the array/string length. Frequency counting over a fixed alphabet is O(n) time and O(1) space. Grouping problems add an O(k log k) factor per element for the sort-based key, where k is the element length.
